beats.trigger: ## Security
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: It is important to stay informed, to follow best practices, and to involve the right stakeholders early.
beats.got: nothing new. The first line is fine, the second paragraph is a brochure.

beats.trigger: The Module 4 prework adds two reads: (1) personal skills as the package format that carries expertise into your agent
beats.got: nothing new. A reading list and I won't read it.

beats.trigger: **Apply** named agent risk patterns (prompt injection direct and indirect, secrets-in-context, tool-confusion, skill supply-chain)
beats.got: The list of risk patterns is real. Skill supply-chain is one I haven't thought about much.

beats.trigger: You've had three agents search your company and three more decide. What doesn't sit right about that, from a risk angle?
beats.got: The question points at my own setup. Six agents and nobody reads what they decided.

beats.trigger: A tool call is not a new species of work. It is text crossing a boundary into action.
beats.got: nothing new. My engineers have known how tool calls work for a year.

beats.trigger: Would you bet your job on it being safe? Probably not.
beats.got: The opening hook works a bit. The analyst paragraph after it is filler.

beats.trigger: Your firewall doesn't see it because your firewall has never had to worry about persuasion.
beats.got: Prompt injection is a persuasion problem, not an intrusion. That is a good way to say it to the non-engineers.

beats.trigger: Scope (give the agent less). Split (break it into two agents with different trust levels). Filter (post-process the output before it leaves). Gate (a human approves before a sensitive action). Review (a second agent judges the first's output).
beats.got: Five named mitigations I can hand to the team as vocabulary. Split by trust level I hadn't thought about.

beats.trigger: Accept the residual on record, or close the door.
beats.got: Write down what's left and decide. Sensible, but it's basically a risk register.

beats.trigger: Damn, this is complex stuff.
beats.got: nothing new. A lot of mood, not much content.

beats.trigger: Module 4 is the canonical place this authoring lands. Taught once, here.
beats.got: A skill is a reusable check the agent loads. I already do that.

beats.trigger: The raw run shows which rules can be checked from files and which ones need judgment, context, or a standing evidence check.
beats.got: Some policy rules can be checked from files and some can't. Fine, but I pasted and moved on.

beats.trigger: Do not go study the policy files before this step.
beats.got: Say what matters in your own words first, then the agent reads the files. I like that it doesn't make me study.

beats.trigger: The grill is wide on purpose: the agent probes both lenses and won't stop at one round.
beats.got: Two lenses, policy and agent risk, in one skill. I'd answer two questions and tell it to pick the rest.

beats.trigger: *"You choose. Optimise for what I can't steer."*
beats.got: A good line for handing over the questions I can't answer. I'll steal it.

beats.trigger: The save mechanic differs by runtime.
beats.got: nothing new. Install steps, and I ran the Code one.

beats.trigger: The policy files are source material. The reusable check is the expert in the room.
beats.got: The skill is the thing that carries the judgment, not the policy files.

beats.trigger: The goal is not a clean bill of health.
beats.got: The goal is to run assess, mitigate, residual once.

beats.trigger: Type `/` in the prompt and look for `/security-audit` in the autocomplete list.
beats.got: nothing new. A step that checks the install worked.

beats.trigger: Expect the reusable check to find things you did not think about, and to leave things "I can't tell" you thought were settled.
beats.got: The audit marks things 'I can't tell' that I would have called fine. I want to see that on my own setup.

beats.trigger: Now work the risks. List them, have the agent explain each, what it means in this system, why the rank landed where it did, what the failure would actually look like
beats.got: A ranked risk list for a system I built, each one explained as an actual failure. I'd go off-script and ask it about the Confluence connection.

beats.trigger: Pick one risk to mitigate. Not the easiest, not the scariest. The one that bugs you on the second skim.
beats.got: Pick one risk by gut, apply the smallest fix, read what's left. Quick loop.

beats.trigger: Risk control is one of the things that separates a prototype from a real production agent.
beats.got: nothing new, but a line I could repeat to the sales team.

beats.trigger: The agent reviews the audit session and compounds one to five rules into the root instructions file for future sessions.
beats.got: The audit writes its lessons into the instructions file so the next session starts stricter. Handy, and I'd let it.

beats.trigger: Give a teammate the skill, install it in their runtime, and they can call the same method without reconstructing your prompt history.
beats.got: A skill is the cheapest way to share a method org-wide. That could be my rollout to the non-engineers, but someone has to own it.

beats.trigger: "I can't tell" is a real answer; closing it takes evidence.
beats.got: nothing new, a summary of what I just did.

beats.trigger: Come to Module 5 without the two missing-check sentences and you'll be reconstructing them while the benchmark is already comparing detectors.
beats.got: Homework before the next module. I probably won't do it.

beats.trigger: Read Mata v. Avianca (S.D.N.Y. 2023) and the Deloitte Australia / DEWR welfare-compliance report (2025)
beats.got: Two case studies I already know the gist of: fake citations and a sloppy consulting report.

take_homes: Agents get attacked by persuasion through text they read, not by someone breaking in. Bounding what they can reach matters more than trusting the output.
Scope, split, filter, gate, review: five fixes I can name for my team, and a way to write down what risk is left.
A skill is a cheap way to hand a check to other teams, if I settle who maintains it.

monday.move: Run the packaged security-audit skill on my existing engineering agents and read the 'I can't tell' rows. Maybe look at my Confluence-connected one first.
monday.who: me, plus one engineer who owns the agent
monday.stop_condition: I have the ranked list and have picked one risk to fix
monday.blocker: Nobody has named an owner for the skill, and I'll probably skip the residual write-up.

misconception.why: The reusable check flags 'I can't tell' on things I would have marked fine. That makes 'if the agent is good the output is good' harder to defend, though I still think most of the checking is for the non-engineers. I haven't changed how I work yet.

one_line: The risk loop and the five mitigations are worth the half day. The intro and the long-winded framing I skipped, and the pre-reads I won't read.
